beats.vo: Hey champ, welcome back! Ready for some more maths fun?
beats.caption: Welcome back, champ!

beats.vo: Last time, we counted the computer way, with lamps that are on or off. Remember? One, zero, one, was four plus one. Five!
beats.caption: Last time: 101 → 4 + 0 + 1 = 5

beats.vo: Today is chapter two of Numbers Computers Love. It's called, Odd, Even, and Patterns!
beats.caption: Chapter 2 · Odd, Even, and Patterns

beats.vo: We'll share some laddoos, hop along a number line, and even clap out a pattern. Let's go!
beats.caption: Share, hop, and clap!

beats.vo: Meet Riya. It's Diwali, and Nani has made a big box of laddoos. Riya's job is to share them out, two laddoos on every plate.
beats.caption: Riya shares laddoos: two on every plate

beats.vo: First, she has eight laddoos. Two, four, six, eight. That's four plates, with nothing left over. Perfect!
beats.caption: 8 laddoos → 4 pairs, none left over

beats.vo: The next day, there are seven laddoos. Two, four, six, and, oh no! One laddoo is left all alone, with no partner.
beats.caption: 7 laddoos → 3 pairs and 1 left over

beats.vo: Hmm. Why do some numbers share perfectly into pairs, while others always leave one behind? Think about it.
beats.caption: Why is one laddoo left over? Think!

beats.vo: Here's the secret. Every number is one of two kinds. And each kind has a special name.
beats.caption: Two kinds of numbers. Let's name them!

beats.vo: A number that splits into pairs, with nothing left over, is called an even number. Every laddoo has a partner. So eight is even.
beats.caption: EVEN: makes pairs, nothing left over

beats.vo: A number that leaves one left over, when you make pairs, is called an odd number. One laddoo has no partner. So seven is odd.
beats.caption: ODD: one left over

beats.vo: Every whole number is either odd, or even. Never both, and never neither!
beats.caption: Every whole number is odd OR even

beats.vo: So here's a simple test. Make pairs, and see if anything is left. Let's try it.
beats.caption: Pairs test: make pairs, see what's left

beats.vo: Six. Three pairs, and nothing left over. So six is even.
beats.caption: 6 → 3 pairs, none left → EVEN

beats.vo: Nine. Four pairs, and one left over. So nine is odd.
beats.caption: 9 → 4 pairs + 1 left → ODD

beats.vo: And what if Riya has eleven laddoos? Five pairs, and one left over. So eleven is odd too.
beats.caption: 11 → 5 pairs + 1 left → ODD

beats.vo: But what about a big number, like thirty-eight? Making pairs would take forever! Here's a quick trick. Just look at the last digit.
beats.caption: Big number? Just look at the last digit!

beats.vo: If the last digit is zero, two, four, six, or eight, the number is even.
beats.caption: Ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 → EVEN

beats.vo: If it's one, three, five, seven, or nine, the number is odd.
beats.caption: Ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 → ODD

beats.vo: So thirty-eight ends in eight. It's even! And twenty-five ends in five. It's odd!
beats.caption: 38 ends in 8 → even · 25 ends in 5 → odd

beats.vo: Why does this trick work? Because tens always split into pairs perfectly. Thirty is fifteen pairs. So only the last digit decides!
beats.caption: Tens always make pairs, so the last digit decides

beats.vo: Now let's line up the numbers from one to twenty. Odd numbers in orange, and even numbers in green.
beats.caption: 1 to 20: odd in orange, even in green

beats.vo: Look at that! Odd, even, odd, even. They take turns, all the way along. Just like your feet when you walk. Left, right, left, right.
beats.caption: Odd, even, odd, even… they take turns!

beats.vo: Here's a question. How many odd numbers are there, from one to ten? Count them.
beats.caption: How many odd numbers from 1 to 10?

beats.vo: Five! One, three, five, seven, and nine. And there are five even numbers too. Two, four, six, eight, and ten.
beats.caption: Five! 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

beats.vo: Now meet Tinku, Riya's pet frog. Tinku loves hopping along the number line. But he always skips every other number.
beats.caption: Tinku the frog skips every other number

beats.vo: Start at two, and skip one each time. Two, four, six, eight, ten. Tinku lands only on even numbers!
beats.caption: Start at 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 → evens

beats.vo: Now start at one. One, three, five, seven, nine. This time, he lands only on odd numbers.
beats.caption: Start at 1: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 → odds

beats.vo: So, if Tinku starts at one and keeps hopping, will he ever land on twenty? What do you think?
beats.caption: Start at 1… will Tinku land on 20?

beats.vo: No! Starting at one, he only lands on odd numbers. Twenty is even, so he hops right over it. Nineteen, then twenty-one.
beats.caption: No! 20 is even. He lands on 19, then 21

beats.vo: Tinku's hops make a number pattern. Each number is two more than the one before. So the rule is, add two.
beats.caption: The rule: add 2 each time

beats.vo: Two, four, six, eight. What comes next? Pause, and think.
Ten! Eight plus two equals ten.
Here's another one. Ten, twelve, fourteen. What comes next?
Sixteen! Fourteen plus two equals sixteen. You're a pattern pro!
Patterns aren't only numbers. A pattern is anything that repeats by a rule. Like this. Clap, snap. Clap, snap.
beats.caption: A pattern repeats by a rule: clap, snap…

beats.vo: Clap, snap, clap, snap, clap, and then? What comes next?
beats.caption: Clap, snap, clap, snap, clap, ___?

beats.vo: Snap! Clap and snap take turns, just like odd and even numbers do.
beats.caption: Snap! They take turns, like odd and even

beats.vo: Now let's mix in numbers. Count to eight, and clap only on the even ones. One, two, clap. Three, four, clap. Five, six, clap. Seven, eight, clap!
beats.caption: Clap on the even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8

beats.vo: Computers love patterns too. A rule that repeats is how code does a job again and again, without ever getting bored.
beats.caption: Code loves rules that repeat!

beats.vo: Sorting time! Seven, twelve, fifteen, twenty, three, and eighteen. Which ones go in the even basket? Use the last digit trick.
beats.caption: 7, 12, 15, 20, 3, 18: which are even?

beats.vo: Twelve, twenty, and eighteen are even. They end in two, zero, and eight. Seven, fifteen, and three are odd. Brilliant sorting!
beats.caption: Even: 12, 20, 18 · Odd: 7, 15, 3

beats.vo: Okay champ, practice check time, just like the quiz.
beats.caption: Your turn: practice check

beats.vo: Is fourteen odd, or even? And how do you know? Pause the video, and try it on paper.
beats.caption: Is 14 odd or even? How do you know?

beats.vo: Fourteen is even! It makes seven pairs, with nothing left over. And it ends in four. Two ways to know. Super!
beats.caption: Even! 7 pairs, none left over, ends in 4

beats.vo: Let's remember. Even numbers make pairs, with nothing left over.
beats.caption: Even = pairs, nothing left over

beats.vo: Odd numbers always have one left over.
beats.caption: Odd = one left over

beats.vo: Check the last digit. Zero, two, four, six, or eight means even.
beats.caption: Last digit 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 → even

beats.vo: And patterns repeat by a rule, like add two, or clap, snap.
beats.caption: Patterns repeat by a rule

beats.vo: Chapter two, done! You can sort odd and even, and spot patterns. Super work, champ!
beats.caption: Chapter 2 done!

beats.vo: Now let's see what you remember. Tap Finish, and try the quiz. You've got this!
beats.caption: Next: Quiz · Tap Finish
